review:
I like to think I'm a patient person, and I've waited a month to post this negative review. I honestly regret not doing it sooner. I waited because the game is genuinely fun to play, but at this point the issues are a lead weight on the other side of the scale. I can say that with 134 hours, I've gotten my $60 out of this game, but I had to actually "try" to get that value. By the time I was totally fed up, I was outside the refund window, so I kept going to get my money’s worth.

Pros:
1. When the game works, the gameplay is stellar. The blending of shooting and ability use throughout combat works really well. It is also visually entertaining.
2. There is a lot of build customization available between your abilities, skill tree, and the mods you select on your gear. There is plenty to tinker with and you should easily be able to find a playstyle that will be fun for you specifically.
3. All the classes are at least entertaining to play. Like every game, they aren't perfectly balanced against each other, but all classes can do all activities with varying levels of effort.
4. The story kept me engaged. There was clearly a solid effort put into it. Not award winning, but not everything can be. The campaign with all the side quests completed, took me about 30 hours. It would probably have been a lot quicker if I didn’t raise the difficulty every time a new World Tier was unlocked. Between the campaign and the endgame content, I think there is enough here.

Cons: This section is going to get salty. This game has so much potential that got blown here.
1. The game, even in single player, is ONLINE ONLY. At the time of writing, the store page says that persistent online access is required for the demo, nowhere does it says this for the core game. This decision appears to be the source of much of the game's greatest failings. There has been a running joke since launch that the sign in screen is the greatest boss in the game, because you can't connect to the servers, or you may just have to wait 20 minutes to sign in. Getting disconnected from the servers multiple times a game session have been a constant issue, something I don’t have in any other game online. There is NO EXCUSE FOR THIS BEING AN ISSUE PLAYING SINGLE PLAYER, but we have to always be online for no reason.
2. Adjacent to the online only issue, the game is peer to peer, and as usual that has turned out horribly. No matter if I’m playing with randoms online or friends who are in the same town, if you’re not the host, you’re gonna have a bad time. Since not only do you now need to connect with whatever toaster at PCF you need to for single player, but now you have to remain constantly connected to the host player as well. This results in ability cooldowns failing, weapon and armor affixes failing, and of course lag. If I had a nickel for every time I got stuck for 3 seconds after using Gravity Leap, I would have paid off the $60 for this game.
3. Major bugs upon bugs. Only the major ones are listed here, these alone should be damning enough that minor bugs shouldn’t matter.
3A. I have never played a game that crashes this often. Sometimes it might take a few hours, other times I get 4 crashes in an hour. After a crash the game decides to create a crash data dumb folder on my OS SSD, despite the game being located on my much larger hard drive. I've deleted 10 gb of crash files twice.
3B. We had character and stash inventory wipes caused during multiplayer since launch, and it was a continuing issue for weeks. People Can Fly (PCF) deployed a "fix", THAT MADE IT ALSO OCCUR IN SINGLE PLAYER. It appears that further wipes have since been stopped, but it took weeks for an actual fix that didn’t make things worse to be deployed. Effected characters are still entirely unplayable. PCF says that this is intentional to prevent further save corruption as they are allegedly working on limited item restoration of effected characters. The game has been out for a month and we are still waiting. Honestly I expect them to say that they actually can't find a way to do that.
3C. In the latest update to the game on April 30th, they "fixed" a bugged mod that should only apply a massive damage mitigation boost at 30% hp, but instead was actually operating constantly. In doing so, they managed to break damage mitigation FOR THE ENTIRE GAME. No matter how much resist you have, sometimes the damage mitigation has zero effect. And you’re not just getting one shot because mitigation no longer works. there is also supposed to be a hard stop point at 30% hp preventing one shots in general, that no longer works properly either.
3D. It is absolutely baffling that the bugs in this game got through quality assurance (QA). At this point I’m thinking players are the official QA for PCF. In the current Reddit thread for the one shot bug, PCF is requesting players answer 20 questions. A similar thread existed for the item wipes. PCF has repeatedly shown that they can’t be bothered to detect and diagnose bugs themselves, and instead players are expected to write an essay for them. Rather than writing the essay PCF wants, I’ve decided to write my essay here as a steam review. It’s fine to ask for help from players, but at the level of help they are asking for, you are no longer a player, you are a play tester and you should be getting paid by PCF, not the other way around.
4. The campaign works on a Diablo like Torment system, in Outriders this is the World Tier (WT). There are 12 WT levels that are unlocked as you play the game and your progress to the next level gets partially removed when you die. This is a good system that would be in the pros section in any other game, but PCF shoots themselves in the foot. WT becomes pointless the moment you unlock the expeditions endgame content, because there is a second difficulty scaling system for expeditions only, Challenge Tier (CT). WT gear from campaign max drops at level 42, CT gear max drops at level 50. Now you could spend resources to level up the lower level gear, but there is no incentive to even play WT campaign content because the drop rates of legendary gear is massively lower than in expeditions. This means that instead of spending time doing the 30 hour campaign again, you just do the same 15 expeditions over and over that take 5-20 minutes each at gold medal time. It just arbitrarily limits the content you can do if you want good gear, hurting fun and replay-ability. Said good gear being the entire point of a looter shooter.
5. The endgame expedition missions have the same issue as Diablo 3, its timed content. Your worthwhile rewards for the missions are almost entirely dependent on finishing the mission as fast as possible. If you build anything but pure damage, you will not beat these timers. It shoehorns you into glass cannon builds, drastically decreasing the number of viable builds in endgame content. You want to build tank, your just wasting your time.

Conclusion: This could have been so much longer, but if by now I haven’t changed your mind, nothing I add is going to change that. PCF, like many of developers as of late, clearly believes that it is alright too officially release a game that I’m not sure should even be considered a beta build. The demo was a more stable experience than the full game. This game has so much potential that has just been squandered. PCF didn’t deserve my money, and they don’t deserve yours either.

I like Outriders and the time invested so far can attest to that. But unfortunately I cannot recommend such a bug ridden game to anyone in good conscience. I will not go through the many bugs encountered, as other reviews have done so more eloquently than I could ever do. For me though, two game breaking bugs forced me to stop playing:

- The _constant_ disconnections from the server. When I am playing solo, why is there a need for an always ON connection? There is nothing more disheartening than having gone through an expedition and at the last moment you get disconnected without any loot drops or resources to show for it. And it happens A LOT!

- Co-op gaming is so buggy, I spent more time trying to connect to friends' games and via versa, rather than actually playing. Often when a connection is established, and a party has formed, a crash to the desktop follows. And today my inventory was wiped clean after such a crash for a good measure.

Most of my friends are so fed up and annoyed with Outriders, that stopped playing some time ago, some even mid-campaign. Having lost all my items is a sign that I must move on too and a warning to all that still play this buggy mess, that this could happen to you at any time, so beware.

Personally I'm rather fond of Outriders - I wanted a loot and shoot game, kinda like Destiny or Remnant. That's what I got. You pick a class, you get cool powers, you shoot some dudes, you get some cool stuff and neat looking guns. There's some end game grinds for item sets and such. I have played the campaign fully co-op and single player with 2 separate classes. I enjoyed myself enormously. 

I think a lot of the negative reviews come from people expecting a live service game or MMO - which the game is not, however it feels like that in places with it's destiny Esq UI and inventory. As long as you adjust your expectations accordingly, go in for a good 25-30 hour single player game with some extra's for end game replay ability you will enjoy yourself.

The graphics are fantastic, the music is good but not memorable. The voice acting ranges from absolutely fantastic to downright awful and hilarious. The gun play is rather fun and powers SUPER satisfying. This is a solid 7.5/10 game that I can recommend when it's on sale.

So, what can I say about Outriders that's good? Because there is some good interspersed between all of the glitches and poor game design and I want to give credit where credit's due.

THE GOOD
-------------
* The lore of this game is just awesome. I really loved the setup and the depth that they go into in all of the various journals and articles. I realize I'm probably in the minority here because I actually read them, but they were enjoyable to read. It was really interesting getting the perspective of the chaos on Earth, the first year of being on the new planet, and all of the different character's thoughts and feelings throughout the game.

* I played Pyro and I honestly found the abilities and how your weapons and armor all tied into and enhanced them to be really nice. Is it unique? Nah, but they did a reasonable job with it and there were times where I had some really awesome combo's that made me feel like a true pyromancer. 

* Some unique and interesting weapons in the game, especially later on, and you weren't punished on ammo like in Destiny 2 where I hear they're still trying to find heavy ammo for their guns to this day...

* There's some great side quests that were well written and had some unexpected twists. I enjoyed... most of them!

* The game is extremely pretty. It's just a shame that it's all looks and no substance. 

Okay that's... pretty much it. If you read all of that, you might notice some pretty important things missing. Don't worry... I got you covered in...

THE BAD
----------
* Not gonna lie, this game pissed me off on multiple occasions. Why? Because the combat system is so poorly balanced and even unfair at times. By the time you're level 22 - 26 or so, you've unlocked most of your skill points and things have slowed down as far as new gear coming in so you can start to develop your build a bit and be a bit more stable and consistent in how your skills and weapons work. However! While you're leveling up, you're replacing gear so often that you can't really develop a build at all and you just feel gimped all the frigging time! Combine that with my next point...

* The AI are dicks! The game offers itself as a cover-based shooter, yet the AI rarely respects that and constantly forces you to run around in the open while chunky boss enemies run right up onto you into short-range combat while their army of snipers pick you off from across the map. Or enemies constantly toss grenades at you or just blindly charge into melee range and start whacking you. As you crank up the world level the enemies get spongier and this becomes more and more frustrating as you can no longer quickly pick enemies off, especially since you're gimped for 1/2 to 3/4 of the game. I dropped the world level to 3 after multiple attempts on 7 and some extremely frustrating boss fights and just mowed my way through the rest of the game. It was always either too brain dead easy or too frustratingly difficult with very little in between.

* The cutscenes and the lip sync and the subtitles... I was surprised to see "Square Enix" with their name attached to this game when I started it up every play session because while I know they didn't develop it themselves... oh my god the quality was not up to snuff. It's incredible... just absolutely... incredible how badly they screwed up the cutscenes. There were times when the characters spoke before their voice lines played and vice versa. There were also times where the subtitles didn't match up with the characters speaking on screen... and towards the end I had one cutscene where the subtitles played rapid fire and were done wayyyy before the characters were done talking. It was actually insane. The camera is jank as all hell and there's tons of awkward cuts all the time throughout the game. One second they're driving through a horrendous situation and the next they're chilling at camp with no transition. It was SO jarring. Just... not well done at all and made it so hard to get into the world.

* They even messed up the quest marker! The janky thing will point to quests you've already completed in an area, even when you've swapped to another quest. They don't let you go back into the area once you've completed the quest unless you go back and redo it... so why is the quest marker telling me that the quest I just selected is going to the area I just completed?! How did this not get fixed in the 4 months since the game came out?!

* There was a distinct lack of interactions with a lot of the characters. Many characters just... popped up for a brief time and then never had any sort of role ever again. They never had new voice lines as things happened in the world and in general they were all just throwaway characters to move the plot forward. No depth whatsoever to most of them.

* Endgame combat is pretty much a joke... at least, it seems the balance was never really fixed. If you're a pyro, just go with a light machine gun with 150 rounds and Perpetuum Mobile. Congrats! You now have an infinite ammo machine gun that shoots fire rounds and will keep reloading itself as long as you keep killing enemies. Once I got this it made all of my other weapons obsolete and just pointless to use. It's that broken. Infinite ammo, infinite healing, cover no longer mattered and I was just a god running around in the game completely unstoppable. Fun for a few missions, but then it lost its luster.

* There's a TON of repetition. The same enemies, the same mission types, over and over and over again. Hell, some of the Bounties you did had the same exact character model for the dude you were hunting. It gets really stale really quick and the final 1/4 of the game is just one area of repetition after another. Tldr; it's frigging boring. 

* Annnnd finally... the game had an entirely unfulfilling ending. Some spoilers here btw! You've been warned. 

There's no conclusion whatsoever... the bad guy that you fight... 3 TIMES... is still not dead in the ending credits. For some reason, your character just refuses to kill them and so now they're alive through sheer plot armor for another game. Absolutely nothing is concluded and the game just sets itself up for a really monotonous endgame all to get you to... wait for it... unlock another boss battle in the eye of the storm to..... FIGHT THE SAME GUY FOR A 4TH TIME! Wooo.... and I think he's actually dead this time... maybe. But who really knows? There's just a few comments by the characters from back at camp after this occurs and then that's it. The storm is absolutely the same and there's no extra cutscene or wrap up in any way. You leave and it's just right back to the pod grind.

CONCLUSION
---------------
There's times where I had fun playing this game for sure! But they were quickly drowned out by all of the problems and poor design decisions that went into Outriders. When the final credits played all I could think about was the long list of issues I had experienced throughout the game more than the "epic conclusion" to the story. That makes me sad, because like I said earlier, there WAS good writing in places and it had some good moments along the way. I wish they had put more effort into smoothing out all of the issues in Outriders. It really needed another year of development. I'm betting that if it released in April of 2022 instead of April of 2021, we'd have had a much better game than what we got. Even if they do continue the franchise... I'm not sure I care enough at this point to continue playing. The endgame has no meaning and for me... this is going into uninstall land likely never to see my hard drive again.

I wholeheartedly recommend that you don't buy this game, at least at full price. For $20? Yeah, it's a pretty okay game for $20. Don't pay more than that. 

And that's my review. Thanks for reading!

[h2]Introduction[/h2]

[b]Outriders[/b] is a third-person looter shooter RPG developed by [i]People Can Fly[/i] (PCF). The game is set in a distant future where Earth has collapsed, and humanity is nearing extinction. In a desperate effort to save humankind, the ECA (Enoch Colonization Authority) sends colony ships across the stars with Enoch as destination, a planet similar to Earth, humanity’s last chance of survival. Here, you fill the shoes of a member of the [i]Outriders[/i] - an elite group of soldiers - trying to survive on a new and dangerous planet, afflicted by an endless war for survival. 

Considering [i]PCF’s[/i] last work on [b]Bulletstorm[/b], I wasn’t expecting much regarding the narrative. However, to my delight, [b]Outriders[/b] has a very well-written and engaging story, accompanied by dense lore and excellent world-building. I’m very fond of how they took a turn with this title and went with a more serious and mature approach. From every character with their distinct personalities and purpose to the dark themes depicted in the plot, it is clear that the writers surpassed themselves this time. 

[h2]Gameplay[/h2]

Once again, the devs nailed the combat system. When I thought they couldn’t exceed their work on [b]Bulletstorm[/b] and its combat system, [b]Outriders[/b] proved me wrong. The game’s fast-paced, fluid and brutal combat mingled with all sorts of overpowered abilities is by far the highlight of the gameplay experience. This game - at most times - made me feel like a powerful being. Right from the beginning of my adventure, I felt like I was a demigod, teleporting behind enemies and slashing them with my energy sword. The gunplay is also magnificent. From light machine guns to sidearms, every weapon feels authentic and pleasant to handle and shoot. All of that is what makes [b]Outriders’[/b] combat so great in my eyes - it’s all about the fun. I haven't had this much joy slaughtering my enemies and feeling all mighty in a while. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2466949940

Alas, the uninspired and flawed level design is the most mediocre aspect of the gameplay. After playing [i]PCF’s[/i] previous title, I was really hoping to see a superior level design here in [b]Outriders[/b] - though I presume my hopes were all in vain. The levels are very restrictive, following an old-fashioned design akin to other more traditional third-person shooters such as Gears of War, Spec Ops: The Line, and even a more recent title, Remnant: From the Ashes. Here, for most of the time, you will simply be running in a straight line, advancing through combat arenas towards your objective. At first, I thought this wasn’t so bad since third-person shooters usually work similarly. However, at the end of the game, I felt like I essentially played the same level repeatedly for over 30 hours - and that was utterly wearing. 

Even with the limited level design, the game has a considerable amount of things to do and places to explore. First off, the game has a pretty rewarding exploration system. Throughout the levels, the player can come across loot boxes to expand their arsenal and document files that provide more knowledge about the world surrounding them. Secondly, on almost every map, there will be side quests and activities such as hunts and mercenary jobs, which will reward you with better equipment.

[b][i]I Have The POWER![/i][/b]

As I previously said, sometimes, [b]Outriders[/b] will make you feel powerful; and that is only possible thanks to the class system. The game has a pretty broad and meaningful class and skills mechanic. There’s a total of 4 classes available right from the start, these being: Technomancer, Pyromancer, Trickster, and Devastator. Each of those is unique, with its distinct abilities, skill trees, and roles in combat. For instance, the Trickster - the one I’m the most familiar with - is a more agile class, mainly focusing on close-range combat, with impressive powers such as teleportation, time rifts, temporal anomalies, and many more abilities that fiddle with the concept of space and time. After playing with each class, I must say that the Trickster is by far my favorite. I had so much fun toying with my enemies, shooting them, and then vanishing into thin air only to appear on the other side of the combat arena. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2466983836

Along with the classes, the game also has an extensive skill tree where the player can spend the points they received after leveling up. You will earn 20 skill points throughout the game to spend the way you desire - with the possibility to relocate them at any time you wish with no costs. For those like myself who fancy creating all sorts of builds, that is a great feature. 

[h2]Performance & Issues[/h2]

GPU: RTX 3080
CPU: Ryzen 5 5600x 
RAM: 32GB[/i] [/quote]


[b]Outriders[/b] has a significant problem concerning the difficulty and balancing. The difficulty as well as the loot, are both tied to the World Tiers. Hence, the higher the tier, the better your loot and tougher your enemies. This mechanic by itself isn’t a problem. It is quite the contrary; it’s reasonably compelling and serves to encourage you to play in higher difficulty settings. However, the execution was pretty awful. The game on higher tiers is totally broken and thoroughly unfair - and this is more evident when playing solo. For example, I lost count of how many times I got one shot by a sniper with superhuman reflexes or had my health leeched in seconds by some random enemy scout - it is so unbalanced that it becomes frustrating. 

I know for a fact that one of the concerns of many people - myself included - regarding games similar to [b]Outriders[/b] is: can it be played solo? Fortunately, yes, it can. Nevertheless, that doesn’t mean they designed this title with enough thought on the single-player experience. For starters, there’s no offline mode in [b]Outriders[/b]; you’re always required to be connected to their servers while playing - and that is something very troublesome, as every now and then, the servers will eventually go under maintenance or have some issue, making it impossible to play, even by yourself. Sadly, that is a recurrent issue. By the end of my journey, I was tired of getting kicked out of my game session and seeing that “Internet Connection Error” message. Unfortunately, it doesn’t seem like the devs will implement an offline mode anytime soon - if ever. So if you recently bought or are planning on purchasing this title, then you better hold on tight to endure the tiring and endless disconnects.

If you thought [b]Outriders[/b] couldn’t have more issues, then I have some bad news for you. The entire game is a bug-fest, with several minor glitches and a few aggravating game-breaking bugs. These range from a crucial cutscene with no sound, inaccessible quest areas, and invincible enemies to even having your whole progress wiped. Throughout my time playing [b]Outriders[/b], I encountered almost every kind of bug present in the game, but what infuriated me the most was the constant crashing. I already lost count of how many times I saw that stupid bird flying across my screen when re-entering the game after a crash. 

Performance-wise, the game lacks polish. I didn’t have a stable frame rate throughout my playthrough; it usually runs around 80-100FPS, but with huge stutterings, dragging down the frame rate, causing the game to be unplayable at times.

[h2]Conclusion[/h2]

[b]Outriders[/b] had everything to be one of the best games of the genre, with its amazing gunplay, entertaining narrative, and exciting class system. And I’d really have liked to recommend it. However, afflicted by many issues and questionable design choices, the game fails to deliver a solid and remarkable experience. Overall, regardless of the fun I had, I can’t recommend this game in its current state. Wait for a sale.

I'm saying no here, but honestly I want to put "indifferent." I don't think it's a BAD game, I just don't think it's a GOOD game either. It's just a game. It's also a game that feels confused about what it wants to be.

 Is it a third person cover shooter? Well, kind of, but cover is rendered meaningless pretty fast as enemies lob grenades CONSTANTLY behind cover, and a lot of areas and boss fights have little to no cover to utilize unless it's forced for a specific mechanic, meaning most of the time you'll just run around and dodge. 

 Is it a looter shooter, all about grinding for gear and drops? Well, again, kind of. You DO get a fair amount of loot throughout the game, but it's much more sparse than something like Borderlands, and you don't quite get the same satisfaction from other "looter" games. Most looter games have regular enemies regularly drop some trash, with a chance of it not being trash, then bosses and big enemies explode with a lot of loot. Seeing that loot explosion is the fun of it, and it's just not here. You'll get a drop or two, maybe 3 or 4 from an encounter if you're lucky, but most of the time it's trash. It just doesn't have the same bang.

 Is it an RPG? Kind of. You have different classes, with different skills and skill trees. However, 90% of the nodes in the skill tree feel entirely pointless and like they do nothing. There's big ones that DO do something significant, but it takes a while to unlock those. I do appreciate that you can respec at any time, for free, but overall it doesn't really feel like there's much choice involved when it comes to the skill trees, at least not until very late in the game.

 Is it at least fun? Once again, kind of. There are some heavy frustrations that you'll deal with in the game, and while I found some of the boss fights fun, it still ends up being a bit frustrating due to how the game's systems work. Every class has a way to heal, which is cool. However, three of those classes require you to kill something in order to heal. Pyromancer is the most frustrating, as you have to use your abilities on something and then kill them in order to heal. This means you spend a ton of time waiting on abilities. The Phase one and Earth one (idr names) require you to kill something in close range to heal. Why is this mechanic a problem? Most boss fights give you no option to heal on these classes, unless you have weapon siphoning or something similar to that. That makes otherwise fun and well designed bosses frustrating as hell. There's also specific bosses I really fucking hated, but we'll get into that.

 My last gripe, and the biggest annoyance to me, is the armor system. Enemies sometimes will have armor, and a lot of it. That means your gun that was doing loads of damage and you really like tickles them. So, you have to use skills or use a "bullet mod" ability. All of the "captains" or "elites" of the game have a bunch of armor, and 90% of the time you wind up using all your CD's, then running away and dodging until they come back up, then using them again until the elite is dead. Since your only way to heal is by killing things on 3 of the 4 classes, you can't save the elite for last or pick off the guys chipping away at your health. You throw your CD's at the elite, kill the little guys while you wait for CD's to come back up, then go back to the elite, and rinse and repeat and pray you don't die while you juggle all of this bs. It's beyond frustrating, and is a stupid system. Just make the elites healthier, and let me shoot them. If I want to shoot things in a shooting game, I should be able to. Don't FORCE me to use all my abilities on the elite, because they take no damage otherwise. It's baffling they thought it was a good idea.

Haven't touched this game in years but I saw the horrible reviews and just wanted to throw in my 2 cents. Yes, it was pretty buggy, and yes, they had some growing pains. But I have never played a looter shooter before or after this game that made you feel like such an incredible badass.

The story was interesting and brutal, and very sci-fi with the classic "the true monster is us" twist. But what really made this game stand out so much was the incredibly smooth combat. When you got your build going and found the right gear, you were a god: mowing down waves upon waves, surviving incredibly difficult battles and making yourself FEEL cool in the process. No one has nailed the "guns + powers" mechanics so well. Destiny 2 has NOTHING on this game, folks. Borderlands has better jokes but the vibe in this game was truly something special.

Sadly, I think after a couple of patches and updates the true game actually came through, but by then everyone had - justifiably - dumped on it for being so rushed, and so it landed with a thud. If it had been given 6 more months, I honestly believe we'd still be playing this game today, but the community never recovered.

In the end, though: it's still an AMAZING game. Absolutely still recommend picking it up and enjoying the story. Just know that when you reach the end, what was supposed to be a post-story end-game never really came together, the DLC was a dud, and the game has been abandoned, so don't expect anything to change. But it's still worth the price of admission for a fun-as-hell base game.

Let's get this out of the way: I don't hate the game itself.

In fact I rather enjoyed it. Played all the way to the end, in fact. But the game is still plagued by a slew of performance issues that can in fact get you killed. Freezes and stutter and the occasional ability failing to go off while still charging you your use and the occasional invisible incoming attack forces me away from recommending the game.

I find this to be a damn shame. There was a good game buried underneath all of this technical baloney scuff sandwich. The loot is desirable, the customization aspects of the mod system (in base game) were intuitive and rewarded creativity, and the transmog system, which was a late addition, was welcome to keep the drip going instead of looking like a hobo wearing whatever he could find. The combat was satisfying, the abilities were excellent, and the expeditions in the endgame I tried later were a nice, steady grind. If the technical issues didn't exist I could easily see myself playing this with the boys after work. But they remain. I've more or less been with this game on and off since the open beta and the technical issues always made me go away.

And the worst part is? People Can Fly has already stated they're moving away from continued development of this game, meaning the unpolished gem we have here is the best it's going to be. It will never be a truly stable experience. Though, looking at the fact that the game has been consistently below a thousand concurrent players since November 2022, can't say I blame PCF for dropping it. A damn shame.

I was expecting a sort of hub-based MMOG where you hang out in public areas with other people and then split up into instances to do missions. But really Outriders is more of a surprisingly well constructed single player campaign, then some endgame dungeon diving, with a drop-in coop system that lets you invite (or randomly matchmake with) people at any point you have achieved.

Outriders labels itself as an RPG but it's pretty light on the roleplay and very heavy on combat. There's one solution to any given problem and it involves murdering everything that isn't the solution. The story campaign is a satisfying length and unexpectedly well made. You have a clearly defined objective from the start, but it will take you in unexpected directions. I will warn you that the story starts off slow and the world seems very small. Give it time to build up. Multiple times I thought I was reaching what was going to be the final reveal, only to have a door opened and a new chapter of the story start. While there is basically no real room for you to make story decisions aside from which side quests to take on, the game also doesn't force you to grind for anything or repeat. It's a constant pressure to go forward and it's always got something new and fresh to show you.

So, nice story, pretty linear, how's the combat then?  Not world-shatteringly original, you have enemies that have telegraphed AOEs, and stuff you can interrupt. Three different guns, shoot your primaries as long as you have ammo,  your choice of three class-specific powers on a cooldown. It's all very familiar to this genre....

BUT it's masterfully tuned. They've taken the basic blocks most gamers are familiar with and put them together in a very pleasing way. Clearly a ton of effort went into making the player feel like a total boss and to inspiring you to build your character in ways that "combo". For example you can cause Bleeding on enemies in a radius when you get a kill, then add a feature where you do increased damage against Bleeding enemies and finally get ammo back when you kill a Bleeding enemy. It's a simple 3-note rhythm that turns you into a tornado of blood and bullets, and there's tons of these little combos waiting to be discovered. Enemies tend to come in hordes and be fairly durable so discovering how to commit war crimes in the most elegant and efficient way possible should be on your To Do list.

Speaking of discovery, near the start of the game you will have a choice of 4 playable characters. As you level up you will gain access to new class-specific abilities, which can then be *heavily* modified by your passive skill tree (realistically there's more like 12 "classes" because the skill tree changes things so much), and then your equipped Mods, which you must find and learn from items dropped in the game. These are NOT revealed to you ahead of time, so you'll find yourself looking at every new weapon or piece of armor wondering what character-morphing superpower you might unlock; my character shifted builds multiple times in the course of the campaign and it felt like a good and satisfying process. You aren't punished for making a 'wrong' build choice at all, in fact the only thing you can't change is your overall starting class.

Once you reach the end of the story you'll be able to participate in an endgame path called "Expeditions", which is basically the same combat but with reduced story and heightened difficulty to let you really explore all the most broken and terrifying character possiblities. There are separate matchmaking modes for story and expeditions which is nice. Cross platform play is enabled, and I never had any trouble finding other people to play with, though the game often complained about network conditions being bad. The gameplay experience was rarely visibly degraded by lag so maybe the game client is just overly paranoid.

The caveats. Overall my experience has been positive with the game, but no game is perfect. A few things that bothered me:
- The game's World Tier is like a difficulty selector. Do not set this to auto-maximum or think you need World Tier to match your story progress: **you will have a bad experience**. Set the World Tier higher only if you are finding the game too easy to be enjoyable. Higher WT levels are for endgame characters with massive gear advantages. Again: you WILL ruin your game experience you focus on this as a new player.
- For a game that wants to get so much mileage out of coop play, especially in the end game, the total lack of communication features is a head scratcher. There's no text chat. There isn't even any in game voice chat for PC, nor across platforms. There isn't even a way to share a discord link (see: no text chat).  If you have friends that play Outriders, you sure aren't going to meet them IN Outriders.
- Do not turn on vsync or frame rate limit within the game. For some reason this causes the game to run at half-resolution and everything will be a blurry mess. If you want to set a frame rate limit do it in your graphics driver control panel. I would think that a basic setting that totally destroys the visual quality of the game would be a priority fix, but reading the webs apparently this has been a thing for a long time now. It makes me slightly concerned.
- There is no protection against getting stunlocked. Sometimes there are just so many enemies that I could literally could not even reload my gun because I was getting tackled, interrupted, and knocked around from every direction. While combat is overall the cornerstone that the game is built on, I wish they had seen fit to cut the player some slack and put a limit on how often enemies will try to interrupt you because getting stunlocking is just never fun.

Note: played solo, maximum world level, pyromancer.


[b] The story [/b]

Well, the story is… simple, actually.

It’s a bit like a classic sci-fi story. It’s really enjoyable to follow without ever being mind-blowing.

On the other hand, the writing is… well, it never really soars, actually. The dialogue doesn’t stand out; it’s sometimes so poorly written that it becomes ridiculous. But it’s actually quite good.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2798568059

The characters are quite endearing, the basic plot is okay, the villains are cool enough not to be ridiculous, the lore is substantial enough to keep things interesting, there are surprises and plot twists,...

It’s a solid 5–6 out of 10 because, whilst it never surprises or reaches great heights, it’s still very decent after a while – but we’ll come back to that later.

[b] the graphics [/b]
Yep, it looks lovely.

I tried the game without RTX and on DX11, with all settings on ‘Ultra’, and honestly, it looks the part, without being quite unforgettable.
The environments are really lovely, but, er… after a few hours of playing, actually. But that’s a problem with the game itself; you’ll see why.

I can’t talk about the graphics without mentioning the design, and that’s actually the game’s big problem. It has no real identity in the first half of the game.

The opening minutes show generic vehicles and people in generic sci-fi armour traversing a ‘plain and forest’ on a generic, unknown planet. Even the first environments are: a war zone with trenches that just look like WWI but on a larger scale, followed by a forest with, er… a sawmill. Seriously, I’m not joking. OK, it’s pretty, but honestly, you’re supposed to be selling us a dream, aren’t you?

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2809644879

The worst bit is that the environments, armour and characters only really start to get a bit original after a few hours of play. Luckily, the storyline’s interesting enough to keep us going, because otherwise, after 10 hours, we’d be absolutely fed up of fighting in a forest in Montana.

[b] The gameplay [/b]
Well, I’m not exactly an expert on this sort of game as a service, but I’ll at least be able to assess it from a novice’s perspective.

The basic gameplay boils down to something like *Gears of War* – in other words, a cover-based shooter.

The added bonus? ‘Magical powers’ that depend on your class.


Once again, simple and classic. Honestly, it does the job. There’s a whole range of weapons, plus class-specific weapon and armour customisations. We’ve seen worse.

As for quests, they generally boil down to getting from point A to point B whilst killing everything that moves, with the occasional objective defence or mini-boss thrown in.  It’s clearly not hugely varied, but that’s why certain side quests, such as hunting or slightly story-driven quests, are there to ‘spice things up’ a bit without actually changing the structure.

The enemies are quite varied in terms of their appearance but, unfortunately, often remain similar in terms of gameplay. The real changes come, once again, towards the end of the game, so after quite a few hours.


The game isn’t without its problems.
Obviously there are bugs, whether it’s minor sound glitches that can be a bit of a nuisance, crashes, or connection issues when playing online.

There are also issues inherent to the game that make me wonder whether it was really tested thoroughly. For example, you sometimes face enemies that advance rapidly towards you, especially as certain types of enemies literally charge straight at you. Your instinct? Retreat. Except that, well, if you back up too far from the combat zone (even though the whole map is, in theory, more or less open), you get a countdown telling you not to abandon your mates. If you stay, you die and have to start again. OK, but why? What’s the point? Sometimes you can’t even take cover, and when you’re playing solo at the maximum world level (meaning enemies are always a few levels higher than you), well, it’s necessary.

Similarly, using abilities whilst in cover triggers an animation where your character steps out from cover, performs their attack, then returns. That’s normal, yes, except that sometimes the delay between the end of the attack and getting back into cover lasts a few fractions of a second, during which you’re vulnerable to attacks but can’t do much about it. So once again, when facing enemies who are INCREDIBLY higher level than you, well, you get absolutely torn to shreds.

And the game is full of little quirks like that which can drive you mad at times because it’s so frustrating. I’ve no problem with my own incompetence, but when you lose because the game is a bit poorly designed and you have to start ALL over again from the beginning of the area, it’s really frustrating.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2815956373

[b] the end game [/b]
Once you’ve finished the game, you basically unlock the Incursion mode, which consists of combat zones where you can earn legendary loot. These zones get progressively harder, and the loot you can earn isn’t necessarily that appealing in the end. Ultimately, it requires quite an intense grind for a reward that isn’t really that great, so… to be honest, I gave it a go and then decided that after 40 hours of playing through the story and side missions, it was best to call it a day.

[b] Conclusion [/b]

In conclusion, I think OUTRIDERS is a game worth playing overall, if only for the story or for playing sessions with mates.

- The class skills, the mods you can use for those skills, and the varied gameplay they offer
- The weapon and armour mod system

- The voice acting, cut scenes, etc
- The areas and the beautiful design
- The relaxed approach to looting (you don't need to pick up stuff individually, you can just pick it all up pressing H, or it'll be auto picked up when leaving an area). Anyway, this game deserves to be played and enjoyed. It has the best loot & gameplay experience I ever experienced on a looter-shooter.

[hr][h1]White, Green, Blue, Purple and Orange.[/h1][/hr][hr]
[i]If you didn't know what those colors represent...[/i] – let’s be real this stuff are in 90% of modern games nowadays. 
As well as that one thing, which is persistent as your neighbor with hammer drill – [b]Trash loot.[/b]

We all have our own answer to [i]“why trash loot exist?”[/i], but I’ve ne'er seen someone who is actually trying to fix it and… [u]succeed[/u] at it! 

[i]“How Outriders done it?!”[/i] – You ask. 

Simple – Crafting. It was made in mind to be useful in midgame and endgame.
[i](There goes list “why is Crafting is great, but it’s useless on low-level." If you read this, then I run-out off...) [/i]



[hr][h1]Gun or glorified magic wand?[/h1][/hr][hr][i]“Y’all got any more of that [b]«Fortress»[/b] mod?”[/i][/hr]


What is core focus of all looter-shooter type of games? 
Right, Guns! And how they feels in player “hands.”

[b]«Outriders»[/b] have around eleven types of guns and all weapons have stuff called [b]«variation»[/b] [i](semi to auto, bigger mag or bigger damage, etc.)[/i], which also can be switched via crafting menu.

Weapons like the Armor have [b]«Mod»[/b] slot, which can alter gameplay. And sadly not all mods are good, and some are to op to not utilize them.

But what prevents guns to be in main choice of dealing damage is enemy scaling (more hp and damage they do) on higher difficulty. 

So on harder difficulty we left with only one thing to do – is adapt and transform our guns into utility gear to proc [b]«weapon mods»[/b] or player skills to slay an enemy. 

Some skills even have strength to one-shot enemy, but pure dps from the gun can’t achieve that, [i]lol.[/i]

Therefore after [b]WT6[/b] majority of players use [i]“two”[/i] type of guns:[list]
[*]LMG with big mag, to proc mods or/and player skills often.
[*]Any other gun that have required combination of mods. 
[/list]



[hr][h1]Build Diversity or lack of thereof!?[/h1][/hr][hr]
We have [b]four[/b] playable classes with unique and thematically different abilities. 

[i]Yet[/i], three out of four classes develop same ability with slight variation in name, color and stats department, and their… 

[b]Skill-Tree[/b]’s is kinda bland.
It’s made out of three sub-trees, all classes have unique names for them but they all do the same: 
[table]
    [tr]
        [th]Universal name 
for sub-tree:[/th]
        [th]Placement in 
«Class» window:[/th]
[th]Main Focus on:[/th]
    [/tr]
    [tr]
        [td]Firepower[/td]
        [td]Top[/td]
        [td]Weapon damage[/td]
    [/tr]
    [tr]
        [td]Survival[/td]
        [td]Middle[/td]
        [td]Survivability[/td]
    [/tr]
    [tr]
        [td]Anomaly[/td]
        [td]Bottom[/td]
        [td]Abilities[/td]
    [/tr]
[/table][list]
[*]All classes start from same spot, with slightly altered nodes to be fitted for specific class.
[*]Nodes unlocks in sequentially one after another.
[*]Amount of skill-points you can naturally acquire from leveling is 20, but to fully unlock one skill-tree you need around 25~ points.
[/list]

If we look at some builds that, are available online, we can clearly see remarkable similarity in them, with exception of one or two nodes in skill-tree, and a bit different ability set up.

This brings us to conclusion: game is in drastic need of node diversity or/and increased pool of skill-points to give us leeway in making more unique builds. 



[hr][h1]Difficulty[/h1][/hr][hr]
[b]«Outriders»[/b] use somewhat known difficulty modifier called [b]«World Tier.»[/b]
Which is heavily modified, to make it work for a newbie and veterans alike.

If in other games new  [b]Tiers [/b] can be unlocked after player hit certain threshold of [b]«Gear Score,»[/b] in Outriders case, you need to level it up. But  [b]WT[/b] gains exp only on last unlocked tier.

[i]”But Wait, There's More!”[/i]
It will loose exp, if your character dying a bit to much in same encounter.
At-ease, soldier! You cant un-level yourself.

Premise of a difficulty that will increase to consistently provide a challenge, intrigued me.
In theory this is good idea, but like the rest, the realization of it leaves much to be desired.
Because despite all of that changes game still just buff NPC stats, but not their AI and/or adding new types of enemies.



[hr][h1]Story and it’s lack of pacing (w/o spoilers)[/h1][/hr][hr][i]“Looter shooters and the curse of bad writing."[/i][/hr]

This one is rough. You can fix bugs and broken mechanics but not the story.

[b]«Outriders»[/b] story had lots of high and lows in the quality department. 
But most of it is ruined by [i]“shaky camera man”[/i], I get why you need it – to show action, but where is the action in [i]“two men just talking a near table”[/i]? 

The story pacing is all over the place. 
Periodically we got straight bee-lined trough events.
On the other hand in some parts of campaign, pacing feels stretched to beyond believe, almost like it was made intentionally to fulfill set quota on game length.

Let's take a look at its rushed prologue for example:[list]
[*]Amount of lore, story and events cramped in a very short prologue is mind boggling. 
[*]NPC are dying left and right, and player character acts like we should care, but we don't since we knew them for 1 minute or less.
[*]We can read more about events and our relationship witch characters in a journal.
[/list]
This prologue has same vibes; as when you are trying to watch new TV Series from last episode of first season and the 1st episode of season two, with x2 speed on.

But how it can be [i]"fixed"[/i]:
[list]
[*]Instead of bombarding the player with text to make them care about all of this.
[*]Make few extra missions on Earth to show how “bad” was on it. 
[*]Including our “fight” to enter the spaceship «S.M. Flores.» (which, we had)
[*]And a bit extended version of arrival on Enoch, extra time to chat with people on orbit.
[/list]
As one once told: [i]“Show, don’t tell!”[/i]
All of this will give players some time to make an quick bond with NPC, and when game start killing them off, we will can relate to the pain our character feels when his friends/colleague was killed.


[b]In the end.[/b]

Game has many issues with its story pacing and some odd staged scenes, shaky camera; however, I liked main story plot and twists – even though they rather predictable. 

If only those people have more experience…

Disclaimer: In my experience, the performance for the demo might not be as consistently smooth as the full game depending on your hardware, so be wary of that (though that might just be me). Also, keep in mind that the game is not a live-service game akin to Warframe, Destiny 2 and Path of Exile, and therefore, does have an end. 

I believe that tampering your expectations is the key in enjoying Outriders as it truly is, and not what it's supposed to be. An enjoyable third person shooter with solid gun-play, a robust RPG system with fun class skills to wreck shit, and despite having considerable endgame content, a journey that does ultimately end after 35 hours on average, instead of being endlessly re-playable like Diablo, Warframe, etc. (which is not a con by any means, and generally preferable for someone like me who may not have all the time in the world).

While yes, the launch of the game has been questionable from a technical standpoint, a majority of the bugs and issues, if not all, have been addressed via patches, as well as a few QoL improvements from what I've been seeing. Personally speaking, I haven't experienced any bugs as of yet, and the story has been significantly engaging (and often campy in the best of ways XD), especially compared  to similar games in the genre. I almost exclusively played the game via coop with a friend, and the experience has been pretty consistent.

Overall, while the game does not break any new grounds, I'm really enjoying my time with it, and I implore both new and old players to give the game another try whenever its on sale. Also, the demo may help you decide whether if the game is for you or not. At the very least, I'm enjoying the game much more than Borderlands 3, so take that for what you will. Though I can't give the game a full rating just yet, If I have to quantify my enjoyment of the game so far,  I'll probably give it a strong 7 out of 10 for me. So if the concept sounds interesting, give the game a try.

This is one of my favorite games. I've been putting this review off a long time, but this game deserves it, with one major caveat: it's always online. As far as I can tell this game will cease to exist if Square Enix ever decides to pull the plug, which would be a travesty. The game was never a live service despite immediate comparisons to destiny, and had a mixed initial reception due to the endgame and lack of updates. I could see the endgame criticism, but it was never a live service title despite the online requirement and shouldn't have been treated as one.

I've played through the campaign and worldslayer expansion a couple different times with different people, and I did the grind to apocalypse 25 for the last achievement. Honestly, I'll probably play through it again in future. It has what I consider a perfect mix: enjoyable writing and setting, engaging gameplay, and buildcrafting that heavily impacts gameplay without being too granular and confusing.

The writing tends to get mixed reactions, and I personally prefer the writing in the base game to worldslayer. The character writing and humor is very dry and cynical, and there are lots of casual character deaths and killings. They really drive home that life is worthless on Enoch. It makes for a pretty unique tone because it is very grounded and cynical, especially for the time when most productions had very overly optimistic writing. The setting is interesting but has a couple key issues (especially in worldslayer) which require suspension of disbelief. I really liked it though and if you want a more grounded experience stick to the base game. Love Jakub, love the casual approach to violence, hate Channa, 'nuff said.

The gameplay itself is an ARPG crossed with a third person cover shooter. There's multiple skill trees you progress through, and you have to specialize between weapon types and skill categories, and whether you focus on weapon or skill power etc. Unfortunately snipers and rifles are useless because in worldslayer they patched them (the highest dps build in the game used to be a sniper build); you can use them for fun but I wouldn't recommend taking one of those builds to really high difficulties. The shooting feels good, weapons are all very chunky and have good effects. Skills look great and can make enemies explode, or turn into ash and blow away, or have exposed skeletons etc. Overall just a very good time.

The buildcraft is really what keeps me coming back; it's very easy to make builds that feel broken that you use to challenge higher difficulty levels, with each level putting enemies at successively higher levels with more health and damage / damage reduction in exchange for better loot drops. The loot has what I'm going to call base statistics, the generic stuff you would expect: armor, damage value, etc. which scale with the level of the equipment. It also has a set of rolled upgradeable statistics and 0-3 mods. The upgradeable statistics are boosted by feeding fragments from disassembled pieces that have those same statistics, and the bonuses stack. The mods can affect your skills or introduce new interactions. An example of this would be making shots generate shield, a resource normally inaccessible to 3 of the classes, or to link 5 enemies within 8 meters and deal scaled damage over time. Mods from disassembled pieces go into a database and you can apply anything in that database to any component, but you can only swap out one slot. You can change your mind later, but only about the one slot you altered, and for the equipment with 3 mods the 3rd is always random and cannot be modified. There are also set bonuses for the legendaries, which come with their own unique mods. There's enough complexity to dig into, with the results having immediate (and highly visual) effects on the gameplay without being too granular or confusing.

You can get the whole package for chips these days, so despite the online requirement I wholeheartedly recommend the game as long as you intend to play it relatively close to when you purchase it. Its biggest issues are its iffy netcode, the server requirement, and a repetitive endgame which ends on a hook for a sequel we'll never get, but they can't detract from what I otherwise consider the best looter shooter on the market. We'll never get it, but I want a sequel quite badly.

Do you love Scifi looter shooters with some RPG elements? Do you enjoy a fun unoriginal unique story about traveling the stars to run from your past? Do like to partake in a wold full of easily digestible lore with optional logs to read for more? Are you willing to ignore some obvious bugs and/or graphical glitches? Would a game that has no pause because its "always online" not bother you? Do you find simple game play loops such as, attack, loot, equip, run, interact, listen/watch some story, repeat, right up your alley? Then have I got a game for you!

If you said yes to all of the above then you will enjoy Outriders. 

Is it the best game I have played? No. Is it even in the top 10? I don't think so. Would I play through the whole story again with a different class? Probably not. Am I glad I purchased it on sale and played through the story at my own pace? You betcha!! Did I leave the matchmaking setting to open for some random drop in/out players? Heck yeah!! Did I take my time and play most of the side missions because I was interested in the world around me? For sure!! Were the check points, autosaves, and story beats correctly paced for an active adult with a only a few hours here and there to play? Without a doubt!!

As long as you calibrate your expectations, you will enjoy Outriders! I enjoyed it for what it was and not what I thought it should be. I waited as long as I did because the reviews indicated it was a good game, but needed a little more time in the oven. I knew it would scratch that scifi looter shooter itch and that I would play it eventually, just needed to be patient. Patience paid off! I finished the main story, played some of the end game, and even have a few side missions to wrap up that I am looking forward to completing. 

In the end, it delivered as expected! Easily worth $29.99.

I wish I hadn't bought OUTRIDERS.

But let me say one thing up front: OUTRIDERS is a really good game, or at least it [b]CAN[/b] be a really good game. It is extremely fun, especially in co-op, and thoroughly entertaining. The visuals are beautiful and the atmosphere is top notch, the aiming is very reminiscent of good old CS 1.6 times, making it very direct and snappy, and all in all you [b]COULD[/b] give OUTRIDERS a positive review.

That is [b]IF THE GAME WOULD ACTUALLY WORK[/b]!

Guys, I've seen a lot of really buggy games, and I'm talking about games like Skyrim, which needed community mods to fix bugs that Bethesda never seemed to be able (or willing?) to fix. Anyway.

The things I encountered in OUTRIDERS during my ~75 hours of gameplay are hard to beat. I'm not going into the catastrophic and absolutely outrageous "performance" of the servers during the game's launch – servers that you need to be able to connect to in order play the game at all, mind you – because games like this often have to deal with server problems when they are released.

What I'm talking about is the fundamentally terrible performance and stability of the game. I really don't have a bad PC (i9 7980XE @ 4.60 GHz, ASUS RTX TUF 3070 OC, 64GB RAM, SSD only, fully water-cooled), so the argument that I "just need to upgrade" is bullshit. Still, OUTRIDERS manages to crash [b]MORE THAN ONCE PER HOUR[/b] for me on average. Sometimes it's an Unreal Engine error, sometimes the game just shuts down, sometimes it freezes, then there's supposedly not enough VRAM available on my graphics card – although according to task manager and resource monitor there's never more than 6GB VRAM (out of a total of 8GB) used. As of today there are crashes when opening or closing the inventory, which were supposedly already fixed in the beta. lol.

In a good 8 out of 10 cases (yes, really!) I can "provoke" the crashes by trying to modify weapons at Zahedi or travel to another area at Channa. Whenever I confirm the dialog with "E", the game crashes. This has now gone so far that I had to get a friend to join me in my lobby so that he could start the journey to another area for me instead. [b]WHAT THE FUCK GUYS?![/b]

Despite changing the graphics driver versions (as recommended by the devs) several times, switching from DirectX 12 to DirectX 11 (as recommended by the devs) several times, experimenting with different graphics and game settings and more, absolutely nothing changes for the better and the game is and remains an unstable pile of crappy code.

If we take into account the other things that could be legitimately criticized, namely: 
[list]
[*]always-online requirement (even for singleplayer!)
[*]bad audio mixing
[*]bad matchmaking
[*]bad servers
[*]bad and too many unnecessary cutscenes
[*]no option for loadouts
[*]no functionality for trading with your crew
[*]no possibility to "lock"/secure your equipment from accidentally selling/scrapping it
[/list]
... then it seems to be absolutely crystal clear what the developers should take care of with highest priority, right? [b]WRONG![/b] Instead of addressing and fixing the many, many major stability and performance issues, [b]THEY RE-BALANCED THE GAME BY NERFING SKILLS AND MODS FIRST![/b]

All things considered it's really not surprising anymore that you [b]need[/b] an active server connection to get to the main menu before you can close the game properly. Yes, you read that right: Without a server connection, you can't get to the main menu, and you have to "close" the game (for example, in case of server problems) through ALT+F4. Think about that!

I don't know what to say, guys, but I definitely wouldn't recommend to spend any money on OUTRIDERS right now. There are many issues to fix and I don't think that will happen in a timely manner. Maybe, and hopefully, the developers will prove me wrong, because as I said before, OUTRIDERS has the potential to be a great game. But until then I won't touch the game anymore.

Outriders is a sci-fi / fantasy blend looter-shooter. It is not the unhinged "high fantasy / rich magic" universe of Warhammer 40k, but rather a "low magic" universe with less common magic more akin to Star Wars, especially if you mixed it with the grimness of Mad Max, Fallout, or Aliens. The power of being a character in Outriders is greater than that of a Jedi Master in Star Wars. In Outrider, your character is like a Greek demigod, with most human beings, even equipped with their armor and firearms, being almost inconsequential. Yes, there are very well equipped heavy humans that can be more than inconvenient, and then there are those that possess some of the magic you have--and those are your real threat. And everything I've said about the human baddies, is also true about the unique creature enemies of Outriders.

There is a main story which, IMO, is well written and pretty original. There are numerous distinct characters, some of whom you'll care about. There are many side quests which definitely add detail and richness to the story line--with the exception of the bounty and hunter quests, which really aren't meaningful but provide decent loot. However, this is essentially a session-based game, set up with a linear plot. So, whether you care about a character or not, this game is not open-world to the degree you can make a difference in anyone's fate. The world of Outriders would provide an awesome open world experience, but this ain't that.

One thing that will catch you by surprise is that while Outriders does have a cover system, if you try to play it like a cover shooter, you will get nuked over and over till you learn that this game is strongly biased toward aggressive, get er done, charge in and blast em type play. If you try to build a defensive character, you won't have the DPS to succeed at the higher tiers of play, and if you play conservatively, you'll get grenades thrown at you behind your cover endlessly, and you will get flanked. You'll also learn that this game has an interesting, and maybe realistic de-cover mechanic, where if you're crouched behind something, and some shooter manages to hit you, they will stagger you back from your cover and you'll be standing up advertising for more. 

As for variety of builds, there are a zillion ways to play. There are four classes, each with 3 perk trees, and each tree has two crossover points where you can craft hybrid builds. On those trees, when you hit cap, you will have 20 pts total to spend across the perks for your characters. There are well over a hundred mods which can be put on weapons and armor, within the rule restrictions of the strict crafting system. And finally, each class has 8 skills that will unlock as you level, but you can only choose 3 to play at a time--I can't tell you how many times I've imagined what I could do with 4. The skills of the classes are not equal in power or usefulness, but their potentials vary dramatically by how you mod them with each skill having half a dozen or so mods you could theoretically throw on your armor. Another thing that dramatically (!) affects your skills is the trio of attributes that appear randomly on the weapons and armor that drop. So, once you take 4 classes x 3 perk trees x 8 skills (3 chosen) x a dozen or so attributes on 12 equipment pieces x over a hundred mods, there are literally thousands of combinations. But this is important: not every combo is successful. Some will nerf you. The game seems to prefer when you find a way to stack the same concept on top of itself. For example, if you take a major trait like Anomaly Power, and add to it with armor attributes, perk points, and with skills that take advantage of it, you can make an anomaly powerhouse. Or you could pick a theme like status effect, something like freeze, toxic or burn, and keep compounding it with additional layers of perks, mods, and equipment pieces that use status power, etc., once again to keep stacking that status effect upon itself for greater and greater multiplicative damage. There are many YouTube and website guides to proven effective builds. 

Another key aspect of Outriders includes the Expeditions, and both the World and Challenge Tiers. The expeditions are session based map runs that you can do after you finish the main quest line. The main value of these, besides surprisingly epic-feeling combat in 15-20 minute runs, are the gobs of loot that will drop if you're successful. The expeditions increment in difficulty as you change out your equipment, improve the logic of your build, win your current max CT, so you can take on more difficult expeditions successfully. The max is currently CT(Challenge Tier) 15. But getting beyond CT10 is a bit of a trick until you master Outriders' unusual build ideas and garner enough legendary equipment and their precious Tier III mods to keep pushing the envelope. The end effect is that Outriders does get grindy at the high CT levels. The game also tracks your World Tier which increases as you run through the main story and side quests. The World Tier, similar to the CT, regulates what level of baddies appear and how good is the equipment that drops. WT also goes to 15, but I've seen multiple characters who finished the main story line by only WT8. This can be a pain in the posterior because it means that you can't just re-run story episodes or side quests to get loot commensurate with your CT power levels. If your CT is 10 and your WT is 8, you will get better loot by doing expeditions.

The game is addictive, very fun, and good for coop. There are some strange limitations to Outriders you should know about, though. First, and maybe worst, YOU CAN ONLY CO-OP WITH TWO OR THREE PEOPLE! I don't understand this restriction--maybe it's about their server performance or the ability to game balance the maps. Second, there are only six character slots. This seems unusually restrictive and I hope the developer will remedy that soon. 

However, as another lesser downside: some folks will burn out at CT10, not being able to solo or co-op reliably against CT11 and higher. Thjis can be from being unable in the short term to grind the equipment with needed legendary perks, or take incredibly long to get, or not being able to come up with the right character concept. You can succeed in Outriders if you want it--I have no doubt. You can even buy legendary pieces on purpose from, one vendor, but the number of expeditions you have to run to buy each one is VERY grindy. 

In overview, I recommend Outriders enthusiastically. I've got almost 200 hours in it now and though I may tire of it before long, it's provided a lot of neat entertainment. It's a great world to imagine in and the human dramas, limited as they are within the scope of linear session and role play, seem real and meaningful. The game will very occasionally crash but in general it runs well and the graphics are good without being amazing.

I bought this game when it first came out and I’ve been around since the early days. I’ve got all classes at max level, and I’m still working on the Ascension points and the Apocalypse climb to level 40 for characters.

The combat is fantastic. Outriders pushes you to play aggressively instead of hiding behind cover like a traditional shooter. Once your build starts coming together and abilities start chaining properly, the game becomes ridiculously fun.

The build system is excellent. Mods, class trees and abilities interact in ways that let you create some seriously powerful setups. When everything clicks and your build starts deleting entire groups of enemies, it feels great.

Co-op is also where the game really shines. Running expeditions with other players and seeing how everyone’s builds interact is a lot of fun.

I know people complained a lot about crossplay issues and crashes, especially early on. Personally I never experienced those problems myself, but clearly some players had a rough time with it and that definitely hurt the game’s reputation.

The expansion, Outriders: Worldslayer, also added more content and pushed the build systems further for people who enjoy tweaking and min-maxing.

Still, I’ve had a great time with this game.

I really wanted to like this game. I was rooting for it from its first announcement. I love ARPGs and the concept of adding the nuttiness of an ARPG to a shooter really appeals to me. I did not initially buy this game because the reviewers killed it for its technical state. I waited until Steam reviews were Mostly Positive.

There are certain aspects of the power fantasy that work here. Abilities feel weighty and satisfying. Mods you get at the start of the game are light years more powerful than anything you'd get in an ARPG. I stacked bunch of mods boosting my minigun/rocket launcher combo and turned a giant boss into crispy cinders in seconds around the middle of the campaign while playing at the max world tier I could. It felt good. It did not last.

The further I get into the campaign the more ineffective my guns feel. I have synergizing abilities and weapons that are the top power level I've been given and it takes almost half a clip to kill one grunt. This would be balanced out if my abilities felt good but only one of them does and it's on a long cooldown.

My second problem is enemy design. Alphas and Strixes in particular. This game gives you a combat roll. I've played Dark Souls and Remnant: From the Ashes, I know how to use a dodge roll. This one doesn't work as far as I can tell. When an Alpha jumps at me (from half a screen away) it does not matter when I roll, where I roll, how I roll, I take damage. Alphas get in your face, jump at you from astronomical distances and immediately cast an ability that forever prevents them from being cc'd. They then commence the bounce house. It's not fun. One of them would be fine. My brother and I just finished an encounter after many tries where something like 8 of them were out. Doom and Doom Eternal proved the concept of "push forward combat." This is "backpedal like mad and pray you don't get stuck on invisible terrain" combat.

Third problem, netcode. I play this with my brother. He loves it. If he were writing a review, it would be glowing like the sun. He has completed the campaign with all four classes, and one of those completions was him making a toon of the class he's playing with me because were are progressing through the story slower than he'd like. I play other games with my brother, mostly fighting games. Our connection is fine normally. Our connection is trash in this game. Did I mention the Alphas and their bouncy castle of fun? Now image that but the Alpha starts his jump animation, disappears for 1/30th of a second, and reappears about 200 yards closer. All. The. Time.

Fourth, the bugs. My goodness. I have never seen so many bugs in a game this long after launch. Map markers are broken, especially side quest ones. Hit detection is frustratingly spotty. If I had a dollar for every time I've watched a rocket go right through an enemy's chest I'd have a full refund and a couple more games. Animations and lighting can be all over the place. Character try to interact with doors but can't figure out how to walk up to it. Quest icons show up over quests that aren't available yet SPECIFICALLY on hunt missions. I don't know why but every hunt quest interactable object always shows its icon before I've hit the point in the story where I can interact with it.

I bought this game on deep discount, play it with my brother, and don't like it. I may still play it because I just like playing with him and he loves it. I'm not saying you won't like this game. But you have to be a very, very specific person to do so. If you want my recommendation, play Remnant: From the Ashes. It has better gameplay, cooler bosses, more enemy variety, prettier art, fewer bugs, better story, and playable netcode. It's not perfect, but it's a far cry better than this.

 Outriders has some pretty incredible combat, but it only feels incredible when your build is optimized and you aren't slugging through the various tiers of difficulties to get the loot you need to make you powerful.
 Through the various updates (and up to several post patches for Worldslayer), there is more build diversity, and less of a "if you're not playing bleed-fire devastator then get out" feel - which has been really nice. Of course there is always a meta, but its less one sided now.
 Outriders is a beautiful game, the environmental art really shines, and I love the combat effects! With that said, despite it being a pretty game, the story (aside from some cool elements) is lackluster, but lets be honest, you stay for the combat.
 Worldslayer is fun, but this expansion story is really short. If you skip cut scenes and breeze through levels you're looking at less than 2 hours, maybe 90 minutes - probably 3-5 hours with cut scenes depending on your gear. The antagonist peaked my interest at introduction and quickly fell flat, which was disappointing.... but again, we're here for the combat.
 The end game for both sections of the game (base and Worldslayer) is entertaining - the expeditions introduce new maps (or areas of maps we didn't see in the campaign) with new fights. I quite enjoyed some of the later expeditions that were brought to the game. ~As a side note, I truly hate the "hold the point" sections in missions (primarily in expeditions), these are long, and if you are leveling and not properly optimized these become overly tedious and a huge time suck.~ 
 Worldslayer endgame promises a dungeon ~ when I first heard about this I was expecting a rogue-lite dungeon based on the description, that shifted around ~ that would have been incredible, and really brought new life into the game. Instead, it is a dungeon with fixed rooms, some rooms shuffle the type of horde you face, and several bosses with mammoth pools of health. There is one exception to this, [spoiler] but you must clear the dungeon and start it again to see this new formation. [/spoiler] If you are optimized, then these fights can go very quick, clearing the dungeon takes maybe a hour to 90 minutes depending on how many rooms you want to clear (not all rooms are mandatory). If you are leveling and do not have an optimized build then expect a slog.
 All-in-all this is a very fun game - if you enjoy this type of combat and the visceral effects. Outside of game-play it has been mired by many bugs, some even game-breaking. Since returning for the expansion, I only encountered bugs that were annoying but not game breaking, I think the team has gotten better at addressing these things. 
 So do I recommend this game to you? If you enjoy the build crafting and power grind that this game provides, then 100%, you'll have a blast. If you are expecting an engaging story campaign with a relatable (or even like-able - seriously you play a total a**hole) protagonist, then you should look elsewhere.

If you decide to purchase, I recommend waiting for a deep sale and to consider getting the DLC as it adds more gameplay and items only if you are going for 100% or want more of the game.

[h1][b]WorldSlayer DLC:[/b][/h1]
It's easy to see why the DLC gets as much hate as it does. For what you get, the price isn't worth it. The DLC's story is very boring and predictable, and I felt no connection to the story or characters. The gameplay is the same as the base game, with a few new enemies [i](basically reskins)[/i] and nothing impressive. The boss fights are tedious with no good mechanics—just bullet sponges, which I consider bad boss design. The items and perks from the DLC are fun to use, which is the only big positive for me.

Overall, the DLC is overrated and highly lackluster. It's not worth the base price. Unless you're aiming for 100% completion or really like the game, don't purchase this DLC at all, or wait for a deep sale.

[h1][b]Achievements:[/b][/h1]

[b][i]The DLC is required for 100% completion, and there are also multiplayer/coop achievements. The game is only online at this stage.[/i][/b]

The base game achievements aren't too bad, and you'll get a good portion as you progress. Some will require a lot of time and grinding, like maxing out 'Accolades' and some miscellaneous ones, making it a grind.

The DLC achievements are similar, with most unlocking through progression. Some require decent gear, like beating the boss on a harder difficulty, which means you'll need to grind for stronger gear in the end game or find someone to carry you through.

The achievements in this game can be tough and time-consuming solo but still doable for most. However, if you can, I recommend doing this with someone else from the start, or best case, find someone who can carry you through when needed.
